title: SHE WAS NOT BEGGING TO BE LOVED ANYMORE—SHE KNEW WHOSE HEART DESIRED HER.
paragraphs: SHE WAS NOT BEGGING TO BE LOVED ANYMORE—SHE KNEW WHOSE HEART DESIRED HER.

The breathtaking confession of Song of Songs 7:10–13 reveals something our wounded generation desperately needs to rediscover: the beauty of being loved, the courage of being vulnerable, and the sacred difference between a love that consumes you and a love that cherishes you.
There is a kind of loneliness that sleeping beside someone cannot cure.
A kind of rejection that follows you into rooms full of people.
A kind of heartbreak that makes you question things you never questioned before.
Am I still beautiful?
Am I still wanted?
If someone knew everything about me—the mistakes, the shame, the history, the things I never tell anyone—would they still choose me?
And perhaps the most painful question of all...
Will I ever be loved without having to beg for it?
Somewhere in the ancient poetry of Scripture, a woman speaks a sentence so extraordinary that it almost feels dangerous to say aloud.
She is not begging for attention.
She is not competing with another woman.
She is not trying to convince a man that she deserves affection.
She is not apologizing for wanting to be cherished.
She simply declares:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.” — Song of Songs 7:10, KJV
Read that again.
Not because it promises that every relationship will become perfect.
Not because it guarantees that every person you love will love you back.
But because there is something deeply moving about a woman who knows she is cherished—and is no longer afraid to express her love in return.
And what she says next makes the passage even more remarkable.
She invites her beloved into the fields.
Into the vineyards.
Into the quiet places where blossoms open, fruit begins to form, and love can be expressed without an audience.
But before we walk into those vineyards, we need to understand something.
This is not a woman trying to earn someone's desire. This is a woman responding to a love she already knows.
And that distinction changes everything.
The Hebrew text of Song of Songs 7:10 reads:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
'Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
A close translation is:
“I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.”
The word דּוֹדִי (dodi) means “my beloved.”
It is intimate, affectionate language.
Not the vocabulary of a business arrangement.
Not the language of a transaction.
The language of love.
And then comes a word that deserves careful attention.
תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah) — desire, longing, or yearning.
This Hebrew noun appears only three times in the Old Testament: Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7, and Song of Songs 7:10.
That matters.
In Genesis 3:16, the word appears in the painful consequences of humanity's fall, where desire and the distortion of marital relationships are discussed.
In Genesis 4:7, it describes sin's desire directed toward Cain.
But here, in the Song of Songs, the word appears in a declaration of mutual affection.
The same Hebrew word does not carry an identical moral meaning in every context.
Context determines how it should be understood.
And the context here is a celebration of love.
The woman recognizes her beloved's desire for her, and she answers that affection with an invitation.
Notice the movement.
She does not say, “I hope he will finally notice me.”
She says, “His desire is for me.”
Then she speaks.
“Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages.” — Song of Songs 7:11, KJV
There is something beautiful about that invitation.
She is not passive.
She is not voiceless.
She is not presented as an object without desires of her own.
She speaks freely within the poetry of mutual love.
And the man she loves is invited to come with her.
Not ahead of her as though she does not matter.
Not behind her as though he has no place.
With her.
The poetry continues:
“Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish, whether the tender grape appear, and the pomegranates bud forth: there will I give thee my loves.” — Song of Songs 7:12, KJV
Picture it.
The first light of morning.
The quiet countryside.
Vines awakening.
Pomegranate trees beginning to bud.
Two lovers stepping away from the noise of ordinary life to enjoy one another's company.
And there, in that living landscape, she promises to express her affection.
The Hebrew phrase אֶתֵּן אֶת־דֹּדַי (etten et-doday) carries the sense of “I will give my love” or “I will give my caresses.”
This is romantic and intimate poetry.
We should not pretend otherwise.
The Bible is not embarrassed by the beauty of marital affection.
God created human beings with bodies, emotions, tenderness, and the capacity for covenant love.
Genesis 2:24 describes a husband and wife becoming one flesh.
Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates delight within marriage.
Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and instructs believers to honor the marriage bed.
And Song of Songs gives poetic voice to the beauty of desire, affection, and mutual delight.
The problem was never that God created love with passion. The problem begins when sinful hearts separate passion from faithfulness, dignity, and holiness.
We live in a world where intimacy is often offered without commitment.
Where affection can be used as leverage.
Where someone may say “I love you” while repeatedly treating another person's heart as disposable.
Where people sometimes confuse being desired with being valued.
But those things are not the same.
Someone can desire your body without honoring your dignity.
Someone can enjoy your attention without accepting responsibility.
Someone can promise forever and disappear when faithfulness becomes costly.
And that is why the woman's confidence in this passage is so striking.
She is not merely describing physical attraction.
She is speaking within a poem that repeatedly celebrates belonging, affection, longing, and love.
Earlier, she had declared:
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” — Song of Songs 2:16, KJV
Later:
“I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine.” — Song of Songs 6:3, KJV
Now, in Song of Songs 7:10, the emphasis shifts:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
The repeated language of belonging is important.
But belonging in biblical love must never become an excuse for possession, coercion, or abuse.
Love does not erase the other person's humanity.
It does not make cruelty acceptable.
It does not demand silence in the face of harm.
The love celebrated in this poem is expressed through mutual affection and willing invitation.
That is worth remembering, especially if someone once taught you that loving another person means enduring whatever they choose to do to you.
You can be faithful without surrendering your dignity to someone else's sin.
And you can honor marriage without calling abuse holy.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent years confusing attention with affection.
Perhaps you gave your heart to someone who loved being loved by you but never learned how to love you faithfully.
Perhaps you were told you were too emotional.
Too needy.
Too complicated.
Too damaged.
Perhaps you began to believe that if you became prettier, quieter, more successful, more agreeable, or more useful, someone would finally choose you without hesitation.
And now you are exhausted.
Not because you have no love left to give.
But because you have spent so much of your life trying to prove you deserve to receive it.
There is a sentence you need to hear.
You were created with dignity before anyone decided whether they wanted you.
Your worth did not begin with someone's attraction.
And it does not end with someone's rejection.
That truth reaches deeper than romantic love.
It takes us back to the God who made humanity in His image.
Genesis 1:27 says:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
Your dignity is rooted in creation.
Not popularity.
Not relationship status.
Not physical appearance.
Not the number of people who pursue you.
Not the opinion of someone who walked away.
And yet, we must be careful here.
Song of Songs 7:10 is, in its immediate literary context, the speech of a woman to her human beloved.
It is not originally a direct quotation from Jesus to the Church.
We do not honor Scripture by replacing its actual meaning with whatever emotional message we want it to communicate.
The Song celebrates human love, and its place within the whole Bible invites us to reflect on the God who created love and ultimately reveals His redeeming love in Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because the Gospel is far too beautiful to require us to distort a verse.
Throughout Scripture, marriage becomes one of the images used to communicate covenant faithfulness.
Isaiah 54:5 speaks of the Lord as the husband of His people.
Hosea portrays the painful reality of covenant unfaithfulness and God's astonishing commitment to restoration.
And in Ephesians 5:25, the apostle Paul writes:
Now we have reached something extraordinary.
The love of Christ is not merely a heightened version of human romance.
It is holy, sacrificial, covenantal, redeeming love.
Human marriage, at its best, can point beyond itself to that greater reality.
But Jesus is not simply another lover competing for our emotional attention.
He is the incarnate Son of God.
The Savior who entered a fallen world.
The sinless One who bore our sins.
The risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His grace.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because some of us know what it means to be desired.
But we do not know what it means to be forgiven.
We know what it means to receive compliments.
But we do not know what it means to have a cleansed conscience.
We know what it means to have someone hold our hand.
But we still lie awake remembering things we wish we had never done.
The relationship that broke.
The promise we betrayed.
The secret we buried.
The person we hurt.
The temptation we returned to.
The years we wasted.
The prayers we stopped praying because shame convinced us that God must be tired of hearing our voice.
And somewhere along the way, we began to think:
If God really knew everything about me, surely He would turn away.
But Scripture gives us no room to imagine that God is unaware of our sin.
He knows.
Psalm 139 describes His complete knowledge of our lives.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that nothing is hidden from His sight.
And still, the Gospel announces something almost impossible to comprehend.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we managed to erase the evidence of our failures.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not mean sin is harmless.
It means God's mercy is astonishing.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means forgiveness is possible because Jesus has done what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
And perhaps this is the scandal of grace that our pride struggles to accept.
We cannot make ourselves worthy of salvation. We can only come to the Savior who is worthy.
The cross exposes the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's love at the same time.
At Calvary, Jesus was not demonstrating that wrongdoing does not matter.
He was bearing sin.
He was accomplishing redemption.
He was giving Himself as the sacrifice through which guilty people could be reconciled to a holy God.
And when He rose from the dead, the grave did not get the final word.
Neither did sin.
Neither did shame.
Neither did death.
This is why the Gospel is not simply a message about feeling wanted.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And that those who repent and believe in Him are welcomed into a new life of grace, forgiveness, and transformation.
Listen to the invitation of Jesus in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What a promise.
Not that everyone will automatically be saved without repentance or faith.
Not that our choices have no consequences.
But that those who truly come to Christ will not be rejected by Him.
Think about the woman in John 8, publicly accused and surrounded by people ready to condemn her.

The passage has a well-known textual-history question: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts. It should therefore be handled with care rather than made the sole foundation of a doctrine.
Nevertheless, the scene as traditionally received presents a powerful picture consistent with the wider biblical witness.
Jesus refuses to participate in the crowd's hypocrisy, and He tells the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Compassion.
And holiness.
Not one without the other.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make people feel comfortable in the darkness.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To transform.
To bring people into the light.
And perhaps that is what you need more than another person telling you that you are desirable.
Perhaps you need to know that the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse the repentant sinner who trusts in Him.
That you do not have to keep defending what God is calling you to confess.
That you do not have to keep living as though your worst chapter is your permanent identity.
That you can stop running.
That you can come home.
You cannot rewrite yesterday. But through Jesus Christ, yesterday does not have to rule the rest of your life.
Now return to the vineyard.
Return to the woman.
Return to her invitation.
Because the final verse adds another beautiful image:
“The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved.” — Song of Songs 7:13, KJV
Mandrakes were fragrant plants associated in the ancient world with love and fertility, as also reflected in Genesis 30:14–16.
The imagery here belongs to the sensory richness of romantic poetry.
Fragrance.
Fruit.
Anticipation.
Affection.
And a striking phrase:
“New and old.”
In the poem, these are treasures the woman has kept for her beloved.
The verse is not directly teaching that our painful memories become gifts to God.
But those words can prompt a broader reflection when we read them alongside the promises of redemption found elsewhere in Scripture.
Because some of us are carrying both.
Old memories and new beginnings.
Old wounds and new mercies.
Old consequences and new obedience.
Old regrets and new gratitude.
And the Christian life is not a magical disappearance of everything that happened before conversion.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships cannot be restored.
Some wounds require years of healing.
Some losses are not reversed in this present life.
But the Gospel tells us that the believer's story is no longer defined only by the past.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
Notice where the promise is located.
In Christ.
Not merely in a new relationship.
Not in a new wardrobe.
Not in a new social media identity.
Not in another attempt to reinvent ourselves.
In Christ.
This is where transformation begins.
And it is why a person who has fallen can repent.
A person who has sinned can seek forgiveness.
A person who has been wounded can seek healing without pretending the wound never existed.
A husband can learn to love sacrificially.
A wife can be honored as a fellow image-bearer rather than treated as property.
A single believer can live with dignity and purpose without waiting for marriage to make life meaningful.
A widow can grieve and still be deeply loved by God.
A person abandoned by someone they trusted can discover that human rejection does not cancel God's faithfulness.
And a Christian whose marriage is struggling can remember that biblical love requires more than public declarations.
It calls for truth.
Faithfulness.
Patience.
Repentance when wrong has been done.
And action that agrees with the promises spoken.
Because love is not proved by how beautifully someone describes it.
Love is revealed by how faithfully it is lived.
The woman in Song of Songs invites her beloved into the fields.
And there is something about that image that challenges our modern lives.
We are surrounded by noise.
Notifications.
Arguments.
Distractions.
Comparisons.
Performances.
We can spend hours displaying our lives to strangers while giving almost no undivided attention to the people God has placed beside us.
We photograph moments we barely experience.
We announce affection we rarely practice.
We can become so busy appearing loved that we forget to nurture love itself.
But the woman says:
Come.
Let us go.
Let us rise early.
Let us see what is growing.
There is no audience mentioned.
No applause.
No crowd.
Just the beloved and the one she loves.
And perhaps some marriages need to recover that kind of intentional tenderness.
Not merely physical closeness, but attentive presence.
Time to listen.
Time to pray.
Time to speak honestly.
Time to rebuild trust where repentance and accountability make rebuilding possible.
Time to remember that the person beside you is not an accessory to your life.
They are a human being created in the image of God.
And for those who are single, this passage should not become a weapon against your season of life.
You are not spiritually incomplete because you are unmarried.
Jesus Himself lived a perfectly holy human life without marrying.
The apostle Paul honored singleness as a meaningful calling in 1 Corinthians 7.
The Church must never make marriage the measure of someone's worth.
Song of Songs celebrates one of God's good gifts.
It does not declare that every believer must possess that gift to experience a full life in Christ.
And maybe this is where someone reading needs to stop.
Because you have been waiting for a relationship to tell you who you are.
You have been waiting for a message.
An apology.
A proposal.
A second chance.
A person who finally says the words you have wanted to hear for years.
And while you wait, life is passing.
Your prayers are becoming quieter.
Your joy is becoming dependent on someone else's decisions.
Your sense of worth rises and falls with another person's attention.
Please hear this with tenderness.
Do not ask another human being to carry the weight that belongs to God alone.
Human love is precious.
But it is not salvation.
Marriage can be beautiful.
But it cannot forgive sin.
Romantic desire can make someone feel cherished.
But it cannot conquer death.
Only Jesus Christ can reconcile us to the Father.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient for our redemption.
Only His resurrection gives us the living hope that reaches beyond the grave.
And when you know that, something begins to change.
You can love without making another person your god.
You can cherish without controlling.
You can desire without exploiting.
You can forgive without pretending that wrongdoing is acceptable.
You can walk away from sinful relationships without believing that you have walked away from your only chance at happiness.
You can pursue reconciliation where it is right and safe, and accept that reconciliation is not always possible.
You can honor the Lord whether you are married, single, waiting, grieving, or rebuilding.
Because your life is not suspended until someone chooses you.
Your life belongs to the Lord today.
And that brings us to a question that may be harder than anything we have discussed.
What have you been using to measure whether you are loved?
Someone's attention?
Someone's desire?
Someone's willingness to stay?
Someone's approval?
Or the truth God has revealed in His Word?
For the Christian, the deepest assurance of divine love is not found in the absence of suffering.
It is found in the crucified and risen Christ.
Romans 8:38–39 teaches that nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
That is not a promise that life will never break your heart.
It is a promise that suffering does not have the authority to sever the believer from Christ's redeeming love.
And there is a world of difference between those two things.
You may still cry.
You may still miss someone.
You may still carry grief.
You may still have difficult conversations ahead of you.
But in Christ, you are not abandoned to face those things without hope.
His grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the power and mercy by which sinners are brought into a new relationship with God and taught to walk in holiness.
So perhaps today is not the day to send another desperate message to someone who has repeatedly refused to honor you.
Perhaps today is the day to pray.
Perhaps it is the day to confess what you have been hiding.
Perhaps it is the day to apologize to the person you wounded.
Perhaps it is the day to seek wise pastoral counsel.
Perhaps it is the day to stop defending a relationship that is leading you farther from obedience to Christ.
Perhaps it is the day to begin treating your spouse with the tenderness you promised but stopped practicing.
Or perhaps, for the first time in a long time, it is the day to open your Bible and remember that God has been speaking while you have been searching everywhere else for an answer.
And if this article has touched something you rarely talk about, you do not have to pretend that it hasn't.
You do not owe the internet the details of your wounds. You can ask for prayer without exposing a story that needs privacy, wisdom, and care.

And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from shame to repentance, from spiritual darkness to faith, or from bitterness toward forgiveness, consider sharing what you are comfortable sharing.
Someone else may need to hear that the mercy of God is not an abstract theological idea.
It is a truth that changes real lives.
Not because an article can replace the Word of God.
But because it can remind you to return to the Scriptures from which these truths come.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a platform around human personalities.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell the Gospel.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, repentance, discipleship, and the hope of redemption.
If you have been walking with us, you already know that the work goes beyond a single post.
These resources are meant to help believers study, reflect, pray, and mature in the faith.
And we want to keep making that kind of nourishment available.
We want to reach the person who has no money to purchase a devotional.
The young believer who does not know where to begin.
The exhausted parent searching for a moment of biblical encouragement.
The Christian who has drifted and wants to return to Scripture.
The person who is curious about Jesus but afraid to ask questions.
The wounded believer who needs truth spoken with compassion.
And the follower of Christ who wants to become more deeply rooted in the Word.
That kind of ongoing ministry takes time, work, resources, and faithful support.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, worship, and a life increasingly shaped by His grace.
You do not purchase God's favor.
You do not buy spiritual growth.
And you never need to pay to receive the salvation freely offered through Jesus Christ.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“...God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that financial giving will purchase divine blessings.
But a willing partnership in helping more people encounter Scripture-centered teaching.
These items are simply expressions of encouragement and support for the ministry. They are not spiritual necessities, and they do not replace the far greater treasure of knowing Christ.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have grown distant from the faith, and even those who are still seeking answers to follow along.
We cannot transform a human heart.
Only God can do that.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word and trust Him with the fruit.
And now, before you leave, I want you to return one final time to the woman in the vineyard.
Hear her voice.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
There is no desperation in those words.
There is affection.
Confidence.
A beautiful willingness to love and be loved.
In its proper context, the verse celebrates the mutual desire of human lovers.
And as we close the Song and look toward the fullness of God's revelation in Christ, we are reminded that even the most beautiful human relationship cannot bear the weight of eternity.
Every earthly love is limited.
Every human heart is fragile.
Even the strongest marriage is touched by mortality.
But Jesus Christ has conquered the grave.
He does not merely offer us a more satisfying earthly romance.
He offers reconciliation with God, forgiveness of sins, and eternal life to those who believe in Him.
So do not walk away from this passage merely wishing someone would desire you.
Walk away remembering that human love is a gift to be honored, not an idol to be worshiped.
Walk away ready to love more faithfully, repent more sincerely, and receive God's grace with humility.

Walk away knowing that your past can be confessed rather than concealed, that forgiveness is found in Christ rather than earned through performance, and that a transformed life is possible through the work of the Holy Spirit.
And if you have never truly turned to Jesus, you can come to Him today.
Not with a perfect record.
Not with a rehearsed performance.
But with repentance and faith.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Ask Him for mercy.
And begin following the Savior who gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Because the greatest story you will ever tell is not the story of how someone finally fell in love with you.
It is the story of how Jesus Christ saved you by grace and began making you new.
The world may remember the scandal that marked your past, but in Christ, that scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
